newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Protests resume despite Milosevic concession.
newsitem.headline: Protests resume despite Milosevic concession.

text.p: Thousands of protesters took to Serbia's streets again on Wednesday despite President Slobodan Milosevic's sudden decision to reinstate opposition victories in local elections.

Milosevic, trying to tame unprecedented popular unrest, ordered the Serbian parliament on Tuesday to draft legislation that would "ratify" the November election results in 14 of the republic's 18 largest towns.

But opposition protesters vowed to keep agitating until broader democratic reforms were in place, deeply suspicious of the authoritarian leftists who have ruled federal Yugoslavia since World War Two.

Some 20,000 university students marched through downtown Belgrade on Wednesday, unmolested by security police who went on a rampage against peaceful protesters earlier this week, injuring more than 200.
But when thousands of opposition party protesters assembled downtown after the student rally, police armed with automatic rifles formed cordons to prevent them from marching.

Reactions to Milosevic's apparent climbdown in a marathon crisis over the 14 annulled election results have been positive but coloured by scepticism. Observers noted that few decisions in the intrigue-ridden Balkans can be taken at face value.

"I hope this is not a delaying tactic," French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said after inviting the three opposition leaders to Paris for talks on Thursday, underscoring growing Western support for democratic change in Serbia.

Milosevic's move to have parliament, dominated by his Socialist Party (SPS), enact a special bill to uphold the November election outcome, in keeping with recommendations of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), looked clearcut at first.
But some suspicion surfaced when experts questioned whether this solution was constitutional.
Milosevic is empowered only to urge courts to establish the truth about election results, not to have parliament decide the matter, said constitutional court judge Slobodan Vucetic.
"This is obviously just an attempt to use 'a political act of goodwill by the ruler' to create a semblance of readiness by the authorities to resolve the dispute," he said.
Drago Hiber, head of Zajedno's legal committee, said he expected further wrangling over the findings of the OSCE mission and "what this special law should recognise".
Milosevic said his decision was based on a need to repair great "domestic and international damage" suffered by Yugoslavia since mass street protests erupted.
A loose three-party coalition known as Zajedno (Together) has mustered up to half a million people in the streets daily since late November to press for restoration of its election victories.
The 54-nation OSCE, from which Yugoslavia has been suspended, verified that Zajedno won without the "irregularities" cited by the Socialists when they nullified the results.

But Zajedno is also seeking a more independent judiciary and liberalisation of the main media, especially radio and television, to level the playing field for parliamentary and presidential elections due by the end of 1997.

Political sources said Milosevic was not, in effect, giving in to political rivals so much as he was coming down on the side of SPS pragmatists in a shadowy power struggle with hardliners over how to handle public dissent.

Pragmatists had argued for recognising electoral defeat to ease Yugoslavia's international isolation and end chaos in the streets, whereas hardliners indifferent to economic problems lobbied for a fullblown police crackdown.
Vesna Pesic, co-leader of Zajedno, said she thought Milosevic had found it "psychologically easier to do what the OSCE demands than what the opposition demands".
Calls for stamping out protests were loudest in the Yugoslav United Left (JUL), a neo-communist party in Milosevic's government led by his wife.

JUL endorsed the new political line on Wednesday. "It enables the political crisis on the streets of Belgrade and other towns to be solved peacefully in the institutions of the system," JUL spokesman Aleksandar Vulin told reporters.
But he warned that once the election results were restored, street disruptions would no longer be tolerated.
"More protests afterwards would be tantamount to an attempt at toppling the authorities."
